cards.statement: Two values of `struct{ N int; Label string }` accept comparison with the `==` operator.
cards.explanation: Struct comparison is valid when its field types are comparable, as int and string are.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Comparison operators

cards.statement: For `a` of type `struct{ N int }`, `b := a` makes assignments to `b.N` update `a.N` too.
cards.explanation: Struct assignment copies its directly declared field values. Assigning to b.N leaves a.N unchanged.
cards.misconception: Struct assignment makes the original and destination share their ordinary int fields.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Assignment statements

cards.statement: If `p` points to a struct with field `Name`, `p.Name` accesses the same field as `(*p).Name`.
cards.explanation: Go follows a struct pointer for a field selector, so p.Name abbreviates (*p).Name.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Selectors

cards.statement: For a pointer `p` of type `*int`, `p + 1` advances to the next integer in memory.
cards.explanation: Go rejects pointer addition. The expression p + 1 fails to compile when p has type *int.
cards.misconception: Go permits pointer arithmetic to advance through adjacent values.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Arithmetic operators

cards.statement: A function safely returns `&n` when `n` is an `int` local to that function.
cards.explanation: Taking a local variable's address keeps that variable available to callers that retain the pointer.

source.title: Effective Go — Constructors and composite literals

cards.statement: Since Go 1.26, `new(42)` allocates an int whose initial value is zero.
cards.explanation: With an expression, new initializes its newly allocated variable from that expression's value. The int allocated by new(42) starts at 42.
cards.misconception: new zero-initializes its result even when its argument is a value expression.

source.title: Go 1.26 Release Notes — Changes to the language

cards.statement: In the struct type `struct{ *Item }`, Go gives the embedded pointer field the name `Item`.
cards.explanation: Go uses an embedded field's unqualified type name as its field name, even when the declaration uses a pointer.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Struct types

cards.statement: A struct's declared `Name` field takes precedence over a `Name` field reached through embedding.
cards.explanation: The directly declared field has depth zero, so the selector resolves to it rather than a deeper embedded field.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Selectors

cards.statement: When two fields named `Name` tie at the minimum selector depth, `s.Name` picks the first declared.
cards.explanation: A selector with multiple matching fields at its shallowest depth is illegal. Go rejects the ambiguous field access.
cards.misconception: Declaration order resolves a tie between fields at the same minimum selector depth.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Selectors

cards.statement: Embedding a struct type `Inner` in `Outer` makes an `Outer` value assignable to an `Inner` variable.
cards.explanation: An outer struct's type differs from its embedded struct's type. Embedding leaves assignment between these struct types invalid.
cards.misconception: Embedding establishes a subtype relationship that permits assignment to the embedded struct type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Assignability

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, `struct{ Inner }{Name: "Ada"}` is valid when `Inner` is `struct{ Name string }`.
cards.explanation: A promoted field's own name is a valid struct-literal key when reaching that field crosses embedded structs by value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Struct literals

cards.statement: In Go 1.27, one struct literal accepts an embedded struct key and a key for a field within that struct.
cards.explanation: A struct literal rejects overlapping field keys: naming an embedded struct and one of its promoted fields in that literal is invalid.
cards.misconception: A promoted field key overrides the embedded struct value supplied by another key.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Struct literals

cards.statement: An existing type implements a new `interface{ M() }` when its method set includes `M()`.
cards.explanation: Interface satisfaction depends on method sets, so a type needs no declaration linking it to the interface.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Implementing an interface

cards.statement: The predeclared type `any` creates a distinct interface type alongside `interface{}`.
cards.explanation: any is an alias for interface{}, so the two spellings denote the same type.
cards.misconception: any is a separately defined interface type rather than an alias.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Interface types

cards.statement: A type implements `interface{ A; B }` by satisfying both embedded method interfaces `A` and `B`.
cards.explanation: Embedding method interfaces combines their requirements; a type satisfies the combined interface by meeting both sets of required methods.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Embedded interfaces

cards.statement: An `error` value holding a nil `*MyError` compares equal to a nil `error` interface value.
cards.explanation: An error holding a nil *MyError still has dynamic type *MyError. Its interface value therefore differs from nil.
cards.misconception: A nil pointer stored in an error makes the enclosing interface nil.

source.title: Go FAQ — Why is my nil error value not equal to nil?

cards.statement: Comparing `any(int(3))` with `any(int64(3))` using `==` yields false.
cards.explanation: Interface equality checks dynamic type as well as dynamic value; int and int64 are different dynamic types.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Comparison operators

cards.statement: The comparison `any([]int{1}) == any([]int{1})` returns false.
cards.explanation: Comparing interface values that hold the same non-comparable dynamic type panics. These interface values both hold []int.
cards.misconception: Interfaces holding slices compare unequal instead of triggering a run-time panic.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Comparison operators

cards.statement: For a method interface `I`, `var _ I = (*T)(nil)` checks `*T`'s implementation at compile time.
cards.explanation: The assignment to I requires *T to satisfy I; the blank identifier makes this a compile-time interface check.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Assignability

cards.statement: A failed single-value type assertion `x.(T)` raises a run-time panic.
cards.explanation: When the stored value fails the asserted type check, a single-value assertion panics during execution.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Type assertions

cards.statement: For `x` of type parameter type `T` constrained by `any`, the expression `x.(int)` compiles.
cards.explanation: A type assertion requires an interface operand rather than an operand of type parameter type. The compiler rejects x.(int) for x of type parameter type T.
cards.misconception: The interface constraint any makes a type parameter itself a valid type assertion operand.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Type assertions

cards.statement: When `I` is an interface, `x.(I)` uses the static type of `x` to decide success at run time.
cards.explanation: An assertion to an interface tests whether the operand's dynamic type implements that interface.
cards.misconception: The operand's static interface type determines whether an assertion to another interface succeeds.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Type assertions

cards.statement: For `x` of type `any`, `case int, string` in `switch v := x.(type)` gives `v` type `any`.
cards.explanation: A case listing several types keeps the switch variable at the guard expression's type, even after a case matches.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Type switches

cards.statement: A type switch accepts `fallthrough` at the end of a case to run the following case body.
cards.explanation: Go rejects fallthrough in a type switch; that statement is restricted to expression-switch cases.
cards.misconception: A type switch permits fallthrough in the same positions as an expression switch.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Type switches

cards.statement: For `type S struct{ N int }`, a method with receiver `s S` changes the caller's S by assigning `s.N`.
cards.explanation: The value receiver s is a copy of the caller's S. Assigning to the declared int field s.N changes that receiver copy.
cards.misconception: A value receiver changes the caller's struct fields directly.

source.title: Go FAQ — Should I define methods on values or pointers?

cards.statement: For a defined struct type T, the method set of *T includes methods declared with receiver T or *T.
cards.explanation: The pointer type's method set includes both receiver forms, so a value-receiver method also belongs to the method set of *T.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method sets

cards.statement: For an addressable variable t of type T, calling a method with receiver *T as t.M() uses &t.
cards.explanation: Calling `t.M()` uses the shorthand `(&t).M()` when M is a pointer-receiver method and t is addressable.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Calls

cards.statement: An importing package attaches new methods to a receiver base type defined by the imported package.
cards.explanation: A method's receiver base type must be declared in the same package as the method.
cards.misconception: Imported types accept new method declarations from the importing package.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method declarations

cards.statement: A method declaration accepts a defined pointer type as its receiver base type.
cards.explanation: For a `*T` receiver, T is the base type. A defined pointer type itself is ineligible as a receiver base type.
cards.misconception: A pointer receiver makes a defined pointer type a valid receiver base type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method declarations

cards.statement: Go chooses among methods with the same name on one base type by their parameter signatures.
cards.explanation: Methods bound to the same receiver base type need distinct non-blank names. Changing parameter types does not create a separate overload.
cards.misconception: Go overloads method names by parameter signature.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method declarations

cards.statement: `type Alias = T` gives Alias the method set of T, including methods bound to the defined type T.
cards.explanation: An alias denotes the same type as its target, so the target's bound methods remain available through the alias.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Alias declarations

cards.statement: Evaluating a method value x.M saves its receiver for calls made later through that function value.
cards.explanation: A method value evaluates its receiver expression when the value is created and keeps that receiver for later calls.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method values

cards.statement: The method expression T.M produces a function with the same parameter list as M's ordinary parameters.
cards.explanation: `T.M` produces a function whose first argument is the receiver, followed by M's ordinary arguments.
cards.misconception: A method expression omits the receiver from its function parameter list.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method expressions

cards.statement: If struct S embeds *T, S's method set includes unambiguous promoted methods with receiver *T.
cards.explanation: Embedding *T brings its promoted pointer-receiver methods into S's method set, including when S is used as a value.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Struct types

cards.statement: With `type T struct{ Base }; type U T`, U retains methods promoted from the embedded Base field.
cards.explanation: Defining U from T preserves the embedded Base field and its method set, so eligible Base methods still promote to U.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Type definitions

cards.statement: The compiler accepts a struct's method M beside a declared function-valued field M on that struct.
cards.explanation: A struct's non-blank, directly declared field names and bound method names must be distinct. A function-valued field receives no exception.
cards.misconception: A function-valued field permits a same-named method on its struct type.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Method declarations

cards.statement: The Go compiler accepts `f == g` when two variables have the same function type.
cards.explanation: Go permits a function value to be compared with nil. Comparing two function values with == is a compile-time error.
cards.misconception: Function values with matching types support equality comparisons.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Comparison operators

cards.statement: A two-result function call fills both variables in a matching assignment such as `a, b = pair()`.
cards.explanation: Go assigns a call's first and second results to the corresponding left-hand variables in a matching multi-variable assignment.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Assignment statements

cards.statement: The bare `return` in `func f() (n int) { n = 3; return }` returns the value 3.
cards.explanation: A bare return uses the function's named result parameters. Here, the assignment to n supplies the result returned to the caller.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Return statements

cards.statement: A function receives its `...int` parameter as a value of type `[]int`.
cards.explanation: Inside the function body, a variadic ...int parameter has type []int, so the function handles its arguments as a slice.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Passing arguments to ... parameters

cards.statement: The value returned by a deferred function replaces the enclosing function's own return value.
cards.explanation: Go discards the values returned by a deferred call; those values do not replace the enclosing function's results.
cards.misconception: A deferred call contributes its return value to the enclosing function's results.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements

cards.statement: A closure invoked after a captured variable changes reads that variable's updated value.
cards.explanation: The closure and its surrounding function share the captured variable, so the closure reads later assignments to that same variable.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Function literals

cards.statement: For `f` of type `func(...int)`, `f(s...)` passes an existing `[]int` slice as the variadic argument.
cards.explanation: The ... suffix passes a matching slice unchanged as the variadic parameter's value. Go creates no new slice for this argument.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Passing arguments to ... parameters

cards.statement: For an int variable x, `defer f(x)` makes later assignments to x change the argument received by f.
cards.explanation: Executing a defer statement evaluates and saves the call's arguments immediately, so later assignments leave those saved argument values unchanged.
cards.misconception: Deferred calls postpone argument evaluation until the call runs.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements

cards.statement: When a function returns, Go invokes its deferred calls in reverse registration order.
cards.explanation: Deferred calls run from the most recently scheduled call back to the earliest, immediately before the surrounding function returns.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements

cards.statement: Go ignores a deferred closure's assignment to a named result after an explicit `return` statement.
cards.explanation: An explicit return sets named result parameters first. A deferred closure can still assign to them before the caller receives the results.
cards.misconception: An explicit return expression fixes a named result before deferred closures run.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements

cards.statement: A `defer` inside a loop runs its scheduled call when that loop iteration ends.
cards.explanation: Calls deferred inside a loop stay pending when an iteration ends; leaving the loop alone does not invoke them.
cards.misconception: A loop iteration defines the execution boundary for calls deferred inside it.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements

cards.statement: Deferring a nil function value causes a panic as the `defer` statement executes.
cards.explanation: Deferring a nil function value succeeds. The panic occurs later, when Go invokes that saved nil function value.
cards.misconception: Registering a deferred nil function call immediately invokes the nil function.

source.title: The Go Programming Language Specification — Defer statements
